Subject: Post-call: Acme long-context eval — model recommendations & next steps

Hi Alicia / Tom —

Thanks again for the call today — great to hear more about Acme's customer support summarization use case and the 100–150k token context examples you shared. Quick recap and proposed next steps below so we stay aligned.

Recap
- Primary goal: extract structured summaries from long support threads (50–150k tokens) while preserving entity resolution and action items.
- Main constraints: sub-1.5s tail latency target for summary retrieval API, high fidelity for legal/SLAs, and cost sensitivity at scale.
- Data: you shared a 10k-message sample corpus (we received the link) and noted that truncation artifacts are most visible in multi-thread chains.

Model fit / Recommendations (high level)
- Baseline try: Llama-2-70B-8k-quant (fast and cost-effective for initial evals) — expect truncation beyond 8k windows.
- For long-context: recommend Redwood-Long-Seq-65B (64k) or smaller 32k variant depending on latency — these models have been validated on our long-context eval harness.
- For extreme fidelity (legal summaries): propose a two-stage pipeline — chunked encoding + KV cache stitching using Redwood runtime to reduce hallucination and preserve context.

What I attached / shared
- acme-long-context-eval-benchmark.csv: preliminary token-level perf and truncation failure modes from our sandbox run.
- acme-prompt-set-v1.json: the prompt sets we used for summarization and extractive QA.
- redwood-model-recommendation.pdf: short slide with latency/cost tradeoffs.
- Shared Drive: evaluation artifacts and metrics (link below).

Proposed next steps
1) You: confirm a 48h window to share a 1–2GB sample export to run full 64k evals (we only used the smaller sample today).
2) Redwood: run full long-context eval (64k and 32k variants) across prompt sets; deliver report + suggested prompt engineering. ETA 5 business days after sample receipt.
3) Optional: 1-hour SE session with Michael to review KV stitching and runtime tuning.

Questions for you
- Which SLA (tail latency p95/p99) matters more for you: p95 under 1.5s or p99 under 3s?
- Any regulatory redlines about data residency before we run the full eval?

Thanks — I can start the eval as soon as we get the larger sample.

Best,
Marissa Cole

Thanks Alicia — all great notes. Short answers below and we'll include the links/benchmarks in the eval report.

Benchmarks:
- Preliminary numbers are in the attached CSV and the Drive report; on our internal summarization benchmark Redwood-Long-Seq-65B reduces truncation-induced hallucinations by ~35% vs. Llama-2-70B-8k on 32k slices, and retains ~92% of action items in our labeled set when using KV stitching + overlap prompts. We'll call out methodology in the report.

Prompt guidance for preserving actions:
- Use explicit action-item anchors at chunk boundaries, e.g., add a short directive: "Preserve action items and list them with timestamps and assignee if present. If unsure, mark as [uncertain]".
- Use 512-token overlap windows with reverse-summary prompts for the tail of previous chunk (helps reduce dropped items).

Attestation / residency: we can run the eval in your us-central GCP VPC via our Private deployment; we'll provide a deletion attestation and a short SOC2 evidence bundle afterwards. Michael will scope the VPC steps.

Next: we'll stand by for the sample. Once received, we'll confirm exact ETA (aiming for 5 business days).

Best,
Marissa

Alicia — quick SE note following up on the stitching concerns.

We observed two common failure modes when stitching chunked summaries:
1) Entity drift: entities referenced across chunks are represented with slightly different tokens and the model fails to unify them in the final summary. Mitigation: provide an entity canonicalization table as part of the prompt (example attached in prompt set).
2) Action-item loss at chunk edges: items discussed across the boundary can be partially represented. Mitigation: use the overlap + reverse-summary (ask the model to summarize what the previous chunk said about outstanding items), and then run a light aggregation pass that deduplicates action items by key fields (assignee, verb, timestamp).

Performance tradeoffs: 64k models reduce the need for stitching but increase per-token cost — on our test workload the 64k Redwood-Long-Seq variant increases latency ~25% vs. 32k for the same throughput. If p95 is strict, a hybrid approach (32k with smart stitching + caching hot KV entries) often gives the best latency/cost balance.

I'll be available for the SE call — suggest Wed Apr 21 10:00am PT if that works for you.

-Mike
